passage:
In Class 11, I joined our school's peer-tutoring club and was paired with Vidya from Class 8. Her English teacher had written "weak" on her report. The first essay Vidya showed me was six lines, full of crossings-out. She said, "I'm hopeless," before I'd even read it.
I didn't correct everything. I looked for what was better than last time. Her second essay had a proper opening line. I pointed at it. "This sentence. Last week you didn't have one like this." She looked surprised. Then I gave her the next task: just one paragraph, with one example. Hard, but not too hard.
By December her essays were a page long. I didn't do anything magic. I just kept showing her where she'd grown and setting the next step a tiny bit higher. Watching her start to raise her hand in class was the best part of my year.
— Lakshmi

Class teacher's note, Class 9, by Nikita
Zubin has failed two physics tests this term and has started putting his head on the desk during lessons. Today I went through his last three answer sheets side by side instead of only the latest. His diagrams have improved: in August, no labels; in September, half; last week, all labelled correctly. His units are now right most of the time.
I showed him the three sheets in order. "Look at the diagrams. What changed?" He looked for a long time. "I label them now." "Every one. That's progress you made."
What I did next: I gave him one numerical problem on the same topic, a bit harder than last week's but using the method he knows. He solved it in ten minutes and asked for another. I'll keep the next tasks one step above what he can do now, and show him the sheets again at the end of the month.

passage:
Monday night
I'm helping Akash from Class 7 with maths at the colony study circle every evening. When we started, he got every word problem wrong and said, "I'm just stupid." Today I noticed something. He still gets the final answers wrong sometimes, but he now writes down what the question is asking before starting. Three weeks ago he never did that.
I told him exactly that: "You wrote what the question wants. That's new. That's why you got the first two right." He looked at his notebook as if it belonged to someone else.
Then I gave him a problem with two steps instead of one. Harder, but only a bit. He got it on the second try and punched the air.
I think he needed someone to show him the progress, because he couldn't see it himself.
Saurabh

passage:
Lab mentor's note, computer science, by Charu
Yogesh failed the programming practical in the second semester and since then has avoided the lab. Last month he told me, "I'm not a coder. I should switch branches."
I suggested an experiment: one tiny problem a day, fifteen minutes, from the beginner list, and write each one he solved in a notebook with the date.
Today he showed me the notebook. Twenty-six problems. Reverse a string. Count vowels. Find the largest number. Small things. But he read them out slowly, and I could see his shoulders lift with each line.
"I did all of these?" he asked.
"Every one."
What I did next: I gave him a problem from the intermediate list for this week, and asked him to come to lab hours on Friday to try it with me. He said yes before I finished the sentence.

qa.a: Twenty-six problems.

Sunday night
Day 30 of my "one small problem a day" plan.
A month ago I was ready to drop the coding elective. I'd failed the mid-sem, and every time I opened the editor, my chest went tight. Kiran said, "Stop trying to be good at everything. Solve one tiny problem each day. Write it down."
So I did. Day 1: print numbers 1 to 10. I almost laughed at myself. Day 7: check if a word is a palindrome. Day 15: sort a list without the built-in function. Day 22: a small program that finds duplicate names in the class list.
Tonight I read the whole list. Thirty lines. Each one is small, but together they say: you can do this. I actually feel excited to open the editor tomorrow.
Next step: one medium problem this week.
Salma

subtype: Stuck in a job that stopped stretching [Actor]
passage: Disha, you say your job feels flat and you don't know why? Let your Nilesh Mama tell you about the bank. At twenty-five I was a clerk in the loans section. Nothing was wrong. Good salary, kind boss, home by six. But every morning I felt heavy, and by evening I felt like a fan that had been switched off. I thought something was wrong with me. Then one day the manager asked if anyone wanted to help set up the bank's first computer system. Nobody raised a hand. I did. I had to learn everything from zero. Late nights, manuals, mistakes. And suddenly I was awake again. I'd come home tired but alive. It wasn't the job that was bad. It had just stopped stretching me. So, Disha, ask yourself what you're learning at work. If the answer is nothing, find something new to learn.

Two years answering the same customer tickets. He knew every script by heart. His ratings were fine. Nothing was wrong. So why did he feel so restless and flat every day? Rehana, from the network team, came in with a torch. "Deepak, we need someone to help test the new fibre routers this month. It's messy. Nobody knows the system yet. Interested?" He almost said no out of habit. Then he felt something he hadn't felt in months: a small spark of curiosity. "Yes." For the next three weeks he stayed late in the router room, reading manuals and making mistakes. He was tired. But he was humming again. On Friday he told Rehana, "I think I was bored, not tired."

I told Madam today I'm leaving the Kathak class. After six years.
It's because of the new group. Riddhi and the others think classical dance is "aunty stuff". Last week Riddhi saw my ghungroo in my bag and laughed, "Are you going to a wedding?" Everyone laughed. I laughed too.

Two months in Bengaluru now. I thought college would feel exciting. Instead, I can't even make myself go to the stationery shop across the road. I haven't unpacked my second suitcase. I eat biscuits for dinner because the mess feels so loud and I don't know anyone.
Tonight my neighbour on the floor, Rafiq, knocked. He's from Hyderabad. "Some of us from the first year are doing a study circle on Thursday nights. Kannada tea and complaints about calculus. Want to come?" I nearly said no. Then I said yes.
Even just saying yes made me feel lighter. I unpacked the second suitcase tonight. I bought a new pen from the stationery shop at nine pm, just because I suddenly felt like I could.
Thursday. Study circle. I'm actually looking forward to something.

passage: Pooja had led the milk collection team in the Anand district cooperative for a year. When she started, drivers and helpers quit every few months. She didn't give speeches. passage: At the city hospital, Pradeep led the housekeeping team for Ward 3. Before him, the team changed every few months, and the ward was often dirty by evening. Pradeep started by learning names. passage: Monsoon rain kept Mohit indoors all week in the village, and every day he told his grandfather, "I'm going to get better at maths this holiday." Every day, he didn't open the book. On Friday, Jatin Dadu set down his tea. "Better is too big a word. Let's make it small. After your evening tea, five sums. Only five. Then you can go and watch the rain." Mohit frowned. "Only five?" "Only five. Every day." That evening, after tea, Mohit did five sums on his slate. He showed Dadu, who drew a small star on the wall with chalk. The next day, another five, another star. By the end of the monsoon, there were twenty stars on the wall, and Mohit was faster at subtraction than his cousin.

qa.q: How many stars were on the wall by the end of the monsoon?
qa.a: Twenty stars.

qa.q: Why did Mohit never open the book when his goal was "better at maths"?
qa.a: The goal felt too big and vague, so Mohit didn't know where to start and felt stuck.

qa.q: What did Jatin Dadu do that helped?
qa.a: He turned the vague wish into a small, specific target, five sums after evening tea, with a chalk star to check it.

qa.q: How might Jatin Dadu feel seeing the twenty stars?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud and pleased with his grandson's steady work.

grounding: In the monsoon a boy vows to get better at maths and does nothing until his grandfather makes it five sums after tea.

passage: During the Christmas holidays in Madrid, Javier told his neighbour Anders, "This year I'm going to be good at maths." He said it on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. He didn't do a single problem. On Thursday, Anders, who was twelve and very organised, asked, "What does 'good at maths' mean? When will you do it?" Javier shrugged. "Just... better." Anders pulled out a notebook. "Five problems after your merienda. Every day. I'll check." Javier rolled his eyes. But that afternoon, after his bread and chocolate, he did five problems. It took twenty minutes. Anders ticked the page. The next day, five more. By Twelfth Night, Javier had done fifty problems and understood fractions. "Better," he said, "turns out to mean five a day."

qa.q: How many problems had Javier done by Twelfth Night?
qa.a: Fifty problems.

qa.q: Why did Javier do nothing for three days despite his promise?
qa.a: "Good at maths" was vague, so Javier felt unsure where to begin and never started.

qa.q: Why did Anders's plan work?
qa.a: A small, specific goal, five problems after merienda, was easy to start and easy to check with a tick.

qa.q: How might Anders feel ticking Javier's page each day?
qa.a: Anders probably felt pleased and a little proud to see his plan working.

grounding: During the Christmas holidays a boy vows to be good at maths and does nothing until a friend makes it five problems after his snack.

passage: In her bedroom in Manchester, Mina had a poster of the human heart and a sticky note that said "Future Doctor". She was fifteen. She talked about medicine all the time. But when her brother Daniel asked, "So what are you doing this month to get there?", she went quiet. "I don't know. Study, I guess." "Study what?" "Biology. Chemistry. Everything." "When?" She didn't have an answer. The dream felt big and bright, but it didn't tell her what to do on a Tuesday evening. Daniel took a pen and wrote under her sticky note: "This month: finish the biology cells chapter. Ask Mrs Clarke about work experience." Mina looked at it. It was small. But for the first time, the dream had a doorstep. That night she opened the biology book to chapter one.

qa.a: It said "Future Doctor".

qa.q: How did Mina feel when Daniel asked what she was doing this month?
qa.a: Mina felt stuck and unsure, because her big dream didn't tell her what to do day to day.

qa.a: Daniel seems to believe in it but wants her to have a plan, which is why he wrote the steps.

passage: At the school career fair, Usha told the counsellor, Nazia ma'am, "I want to be a doctor." Nazia ma'am smiled. "Wonderful. What are you doing this month for it?" Usha blinked. She'd wanted to be a doctor since Class 5. She had a stethoscope keychain. But this month? "Studying," she said. "Which part?" Usha looked down. "I haven't really started. It feels so far away." Nazia ma'am pulled out a small planner. "A far dream is like a star. It tells you the direction. But you walk with small steps." Together they wrote three things for the month: finish two biology chapters, do one chemistry test paper each week, and talk to Usha's aunt, who is a nurse, about hospital life. Usha stared at the list. "That's it?" "For this month. Next month, three more." Usha left the fair holding the planner like a map.

qa.q: Since which class had Usha wanted to be a doctor?
qa.a: Since Class 5.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when asked what she was doing this month?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed and stuck, because the dream felt so far away that she hadn't really started.

qa.q: What did Nazia ma'am help Usha do, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She helped Usha write three near steps for the month, so the distant goal could guide daily action.

qa.q: How might Usha's aunt, the nurse, help Usha?
qa.a: Her aunt could share real stories of hospital life, making the dream feel closer and clearer.

grounding: A teenager dreams of being a doctor but has no plan for the month, and a counsellor helps her break it into near steps.
